## Introduction

1.1 Motivation

The end of Moore’s law creates a demand for novel ways to meet the speed, cost,

and energy requirements in novel application domains as well as for established ap-

plication domains. One of the key layers to achieve progress in this area is through

hardware/software co-design and relying on hardware accelerators to deliver orders of

1


<!-- Page 17 -->


magnitude of PPA improvements.

Accelerators are implemented using limited area budgets, allowing few applications

to benefit from acceleration. Moreover, designers rely on their intuitions of where the

bottlenecks are in the applications they accelerate. They rely on software profiling

tools that are helpful for CPU optimizations but very limited for designing future

systems that contain CPUs and accelerators. Software profiling-driven acceleration of

program regions is agnostic of the CPU-accelerator connection latency and bandwidth

requirements as well as the area cost of the accelerated region. Consequently, early in

the SoC design stages, designers partition their applications sub-optimally and start

time-consuming iterative synthesis and accelerator optimization flows, which deliver

far-from-optimal system-wide PPA results. Throughout this dissertation, we label

early-stage design space exploration as EDSE.

Previous solutions have attempted to create application analysis tools that provide

early-stage system design information, but they lack in three important dimensions.

• A) Co-design of the hardware models for PPA and the optimization models.

Since the application is not in an HLS-friendly format or partitioned in the

early stages, the early-stage design tools must rely on models for partitioning

the application and effective area reuse insights. Those related work tools do

not analyze the effect of relying on models for the PPA rather than completely

accurate information. In this thesis, we show that the impact on the end-to-

end EDSE reports and their effectiveness in achieving optimal partitioning is

severely affected by this lack of model study.

• B) Early-DSE that uses significant late-stage information. Most tools that at-

tempt EDSE rely on significant late-stage design information, such as reports

2


<!-- Page 18 -->


from HLS tools or even the premature specification of highly optimized acceler-

ator implementation, resulting in suboptimal system design choices and defeat-

ing the purpose of early-stage design space exploration.

• C) Lack of control and data-flow graph (CDFG) pattern detection and granu-

larity optimization. The granularity at which many non-conventional acceler-

ators are being designed, including area-reusing accelerators and accelerators

resulting from automated hardware-software partitioning, is too fine-grained,

most notably at the basic blocks or loop granularity in the best case.

In this thesis, we propose early-stage solutions for designing non-conventional ac-

celerators that address the suboptimality problems in early-stage system partitioning

and increase the application size/number of applications that can be accelerated per

chip. First, with AccelMerger, we address the EDSE with area reuse in mind to pro-

duce highly eﬀicient accelerators. We use code merging techniques prior to high-level

synthesis to achieve circuitry reuse, and we select profitable merged circuitry not just

in terms of its PPA tradeoffs but also in terms of the data communication require-

ments. Second, we analyze the potential for creating multi-application accelerators

by merging application regions and then synthesizing those merged regions to cre-

ate area and energy-eﬀicient accelerators. We build Guac, a tool relying on sequence

alignment compiler transformations to achieve these PPA improvements inter- and

intra-application while analyzing the impact of statistical PPA models in sequence

alignment techniques. Third, we analyze the limitations in early-stage design space

exploration regarding optimality and error, starting from non-optimized application

implementation. We developed Accura-EDSE, a tool that accurately performs early-

stage design space exploration.

3


<!-- Page 19 -->


For all these solutions, we (A) perform extensive accuracy research both for accel-

erator selection as well as for circuitry reuse, (B) make them available at the early

stages of design by employing a validated statistical methodology, and (C) operate at

flexible granularities, from loop level to hierarchies of function calls.

### 1.2 Background

The 90s and the emergence of high-level synthesis. In the 90s, high-level synthesis re-

search emerged to cope with the increasing complexity of hardware accelerator de-

sign17,18,35. In the same way that compilers elevated the level of abstraction from

CPU assembly language, designing hardware accelerators, described with register-

transfer level (RTL) code, could be simplified starting from a high-level language, too.

Another motivation for HLS in the 90s was using digital signal processors (DSPs),

which could accelerate at a good performance per watt floating point operation. HLS

progressed alongside single-core CPU architectural improvements during that decade.

Surprisingly, the typical HLS stages of allocation, scheduling, and binding have re-

mained the same over the decades, with progress focused on supporting different ar-

chitectures and high-level languages. Recently, HLS tools have progressed to cover

high-level representations of code with more parallelism and data locality information

by focusing on a particular domain such as ML77,36 while still supporting applications

written in general-purpose languages like C/C++.

In the 2000s, fine-grained resource sharing and instruction set extensions. In the

2000-2010 period, single-core performance reached its peak, and multi-cores were

chosen as a way to continue extracting performance from the increasing number of

transistors per unit of area. Cores were also becoming more complex by adding fine-

4


<!-- Page 20 -->


grained accelerators in addition to aggressively deep pipelines. This materialized in

the Instruction Set Extension (ISE) literature39,4,69,66,49,10,45, which was looking for

more complex patterns in programs, namely data-flow graphs (DFGs). In the 90s, the

patterns searched were just a few instructions so the DSPs could be leveraged effec-

tively at the right granularity. The research in ISE started using more sophisticated

techniques to match longer strings of instructions. This ISE research literature con-

tinued to be important in the 2010s research, which focused on applications64,33,57.

However, to our knowledge, tightly coupled fine-grained accelerators were not adopted

commercially for CPUs, at least not the kind created via automatic code/circuit

matching methodology. The reason ISE with fine-grained merged accelerators was not

implemented commercially is beyond the scope of this dissertation. Still, we think the

cause was the RISC criticism of complex instructions as well as the already diﬀicult

task of verification and validation of CPUs.

The 2010s, the ML boom, and domain-specific fine-grained ISE. In the early 2010s,

Machine Learning saw a lot of success with the introduction of the ImageNet dataset

and AlexNet convolutional neural network, as well as in the language domain with

Seq2Seq. The computer architecture community soon started manually designing ac-

celerators for ML9,30. EDSE, neither for partitioning nor for merging, was being used

yet, so the designer had to rely on their intuition as to which patterns were worth ac-

celerating across multiple applications and what the right granularity was at which

to create those accelerators. These were loosely coupled coarse-grained accelerators

connected to the CPU via AXI-style interconnect. This early information that accel-

erators would be more favorably designed in a loosely coupled fashion was not imme-

diately leveraged in the design automation research. This led to the continued push

for ISE extensions in the early 2010s Conservation Cores (CCORES)67 and Quasi-

5


<!-- Page 21 -->


Specific Cores (QSCORES)68 which showed the improved energy eﬀiciency of fine-

grained merged accelerators tightly coupled with CPUs. Another major limitation of

these tools was the language coverage, as they were designed for functions with aﬀine

behavior, mostly mathematical functions that could be expressed with a few loops

and were easy to analyze for patterns. Those late-stage DSE tools could only benefit

from computational pattern reuse post-hardware-software partitioning.

Late 2010s, early 2020s, domain-specific accelerators, and ML-assisted DSE. In the

late 2010s and early 2020s, inspired by how accelerators were designed in a loosely-

coupled fashion led to early-stage system design tools26,80,79,78 as well as tools that

detected merging opportunities at coarser granularities37, though in the latter case

inheriting language limitations similar to the ones in late-stage merging tools such as

QSCORES. Developing coarse-grained merging at the level of the C/C++/Abstract-

Syntax-Tree level had the limitation that each statement or instruction can be ar-

bitrarily complex, whereas, in the IR, each instruction is expressed in a short pre-

determined format very amenable for optimizations like function merging. This is an

important reason why most optimizations are implemented at the IR level), being

limited to small kernels and without analysis of the impact of models either in the

selection or the merging problem. A significant development was the emergence of

function-merging techniques52,50,51 in the compilers community, which support arbi-

trary granularities in the source code for merging. This dissertation aims to further

the early-stage design of coarse-grained merged accelerators, leveraging optimization

methods, function merging by sequence alignment compiler techniques, and statistical

learning for the next generation of EDSE tools.

In the same period, a number of late DSE and other solutions in between the early

and late stages have been developed. gem5-aladdin55 and gem5-salam53 have been

6


<!-- Page 22 -->


developed for cycle-accurate simulation and less focus on design space exploration.

Several works have focused on the design space exploration problem, such as Arch-

Gym25 on using Reinforcement Learning (RL) and other optimization methodologies

to explore memory and DNN accelerator designs. Other approaches include employing

Bayesian optimization48,2,25 or transforming the discrete design space into a contin-

uous representation to apply fast traditional optimization approaches as in the case

of Vaesa21. In order to search for globally optimum solutions, in this dissertation, we

focus on mixed integer programming optimization to explore the early-stage design

space of hardware-software partitioning and computational pattern reuse.

1.3 Approaches to EDSE

In this dissertation, we split related work into four categories. The following types of

tools and methodologies are relevant to the EDSE discussion since they are used prac-

tically for early-stage design, even if, in most cases, they were not originally designed

for EDSE.

• Manual Design is still the prevalent way of designing hardware while relying on

standard profiling tools such as gprof to identify hotspots, followed by manual

application translation to a hardware description language such as Verilog. The

drawback of this approach is that it needs to make many design assumptions

regarding the optimal acceleration granularity and the partitioning of the appli-

cation into software and hardware that will minimize CPU-accelerator commu-

nication.

• HLS is a higher-level way of doing architectural exploration since it only re-

quires the application to be in a synthesizable format. If that is the case, the

7


<!-- Page 23 -->


HLS ecosystem can provide co-simulation tools, which allow the designer to

make architectural choices when combined with standard CPU profiling. The

issue with this approach is that transforming the application to a synthesizable

format still requires significant manual application changes, such as expressing

memory accesses to (ideally statically allocated) array-style data structures in-

stead of, for example, templated vector data structures, rewriting the code with

no side-effects in the functions of interest for acceleration, and other simplifica-

tions such as the prohibitive use of object-oriented-programming. Additionally,

HLS-style co-simulation takes excessive time for architectural explorations that

perform fine-grained merging and search for optimal hardware-software parti-

tionings.

• LateDSE. Here, we refer to the set of tools and frameworks that allow cycle-

accurate simulation (e.g. gem5-aladdin), analytical simulations based on high-

fidelity characterizations of software kernels on different hardware targets (e.g.

Synopsys Platform Architect), as well as the ISE approaches, which accelerate

at fine granularities. We call them LateDSE since the accelerated application

regions still have significant code transformation requirements but do not re-

quire producing an implementation for the accelerated regions. The accelerated

regions are emulated on specific hardware from their original high-level descrip-

tion. This approach is faster than HLS, but compared to the time budget of a

few minutes per design (required in EDSE), it is very limited in terms of agile

architectural exploration.

• OtherEDSE Other EDSE tools than the ones presented in this dissertation

achieve the versatility and speed required for architectural exploration. Several

8


<!-- Page 24 -->


drawbacks prevented the widespread adoption of EDSE tools, including the lack

of analysis of the interaction between hardware cost models and DSE errors.

Other desirable features of EDSE are that, even though it is technically possible

to analyze application patterns and granularities, related tools offer limited sup-

port for identifying non-conventional acceleration candidates that can accelerate

multiple workloads.

## 2

## Early DSE and Automatic Generation of

## Coarse Grained Merged Accelerators

Post-Moore’s law area-constrained systems rely on accelerators to deliver performance

enhancements. Coarse-grained accelerators can offer substantial domain acceleration,

but manual, ad-hoc identification of code to accelerate is prohibitively expensive.

Because cycle-accurate simulators and high-level synthesis (HLS) flows are so time-

14


<!-- Page 30 -->


consuming, the manual creation of high-utilization accelerators that exploit control

and data flow patterns at optimal granularities is rarely successful. To address these

challenges, we present AccelMerger, the first automated methodology to create coarse-

grained, control- and data-flow-rich merged accelerators. AccelMerger uses sequence

alignment matching to recognize similar function call-graphs and loops, and neural

networks to quickly evaluate their post-HLS characteristics. It accurately identifies

which functions to accelerate, and it merges accelerators to respect an area budget

and to accommodate system communication characteristics like latency and band-

width. Merging two accelerators can save as much as 99% of the area of one. The

space saved is used by a globally optimal integer linear program to allocate more

accelerators for increased performance. We demonstrate AccelMerger’s effectiveness

using HLS flows without any manual effort to fine-tune the resulting designs. On

FPGA-based systems, AccelMerger yields application performance improvements of

up to 16.7× over software implementations, and 1.91× on average with respect to

state-of-the-art early-stage design space exploration tools.

2.1 Motivation

As CMOS scaling slows, the increase in micro-circuitry per unit area, deciding which

code regions to accelerate becomes harder. However, the demand for improved per-

formance is exacerbated by novel domains such as AR/VR, Robotics, and Machine

Learning that require more agile and eﬀicient design methodologies. The traditional

approach in accelerating novel applications is to manually profile them and decide in

an ad-hoc manner what code regions should be mapped onto hardware. These man-

ual approaches are ad-hoc since they either directly map specific functions or loops

15


<!-- Page 31 -->


onto hardware at a fixed granularity60 and/or informally identify a simple pattern oc-

curring across different functions and create an accelerator for that (e.g.9,30). Code

patterns can be as simple as repeated sequences of multiply-add operations to com-

plex control flow graphs (CFGs) and data flow graphs (DFGs) representing a function

(CDFG) or a function call graph (nested-CDFG). In the case of manual accelerator

design, patterns are only exploited at fine basic-block/DFG-level granularities, based

on the architect’s domain intuition.

To overcome some of these manual aspects of accelerator design, Early-Stage De-

sign Space Exploration (Early-DSE)80,79,26 has emerged as a profiling methodology

able to discover new SoC architectures adjusted to the application’s characteristics.

Furthermore, Early-DSE informs the SoC designer without having to manually trans-

form the most executed application functions into a synthesizable format, i.e. accept-

able by HLS Tools7,44,73,6, an extremely error-prone and time-consuming process.

However, Early-DSE comes unprepared to exploit variable CDFG granularities and

much less to reason about architectures that reuse CDFG logic.

Merging small/fine-grained DFGs68,64,39,10 have been implemented using a graph-

isomorphism approach, at HLS time, therefore missing an opportunity to think about

the whole system in terms of reusing CDFG patterns. These approaches have received

limited adoption in RTL synthesis tools44 7, most likely because graph-isomorphism

is NP-Hard and not very scalable. Additionally, at fine granularities, the benefits of

calling an accelerator are greatly diminished by the cost of updating and reading from

a register file (RF). Similarly, fine-grained merged accelerators tend to be tightly cou-

pled with the general purpose core, for example via the cache memory system. In the

HLS context, RF-less, coarse-grained accelerators have had the most success since rich

CDFGs are mapped to hardware via datapaths handled via control logic. There is no

2.3 Problem Definition

Vanilla HW/SW Partitioning. We first describe the vanilla HW/SW partitioning

problem as addressed in the related work and then proceed to the larger problem

present in systems with limited area resources. Given a set of functions P = {f1, .., fn},

23


<!-- Page 39 -->


each best represented by a CDFG, a list of arguments and a returned type, the vanilla

HW/SW partitioning generates two sets of functions A = {fi1, .., fip} and B = {fj1, .., fjq}

to execute on a general-purpose core and on specialized hardware, respectively. The

two sets represent a partitioning of P since A ∩B = ∅and A ∪B = P. This partitioning

is done by maximizing program performance subject to the total resource require-

ments of the accelerators and the general-purpose CPU, along with a description of

how these components communicate. The related work in early-stage DSE80,79 oper-

ates on parameters swi, hwi, and areai, which are automatically determined for each

function. swi and hwi represent the overall time spent in seconds executing a func-

tion in software, using a general-purpose core, and in hardware, using coarse-grained

accelerators, respectively. areai is the area requirement per component measured in

Lookup Tables (LUTs). Some uncommon features that are usually only modeled in

late-stage DSE tools, such as gem5-aladdin56 and gem5-salam53, are the interconnect

latency and bandwidth that provide insights about the system level, and we take these

into account when determining the optimal partitioning. In contrast with late-stage

DSE, which is focused on evaluating point-solution SoC designs with the predefined

set of functions to accelerate and run in software, we need an agile way of determining

which loops and functions to accelerate and merge.

2.6.2 Accelerator invocation latency impact

Several factors can hurt the performance attainable via acceleration. Applications

with high numbers of calls, for the most significant functions, tend to suffer from

communication costs, since for each invocation of an accelerator, the host needs to

set up memory-mapped model-specific registers (MSRs), and the accelerator notifies

the host when the accelerated function and all its callees have finished. Beyond the

large gap between memory access time and compute72, and system configurations

with off-chip FPGAs, long cache flushes are required before offloading computation

onto accelerators56.

Any of these scenarios can lead to high latency in initiating communication with

the accelerator. In Figure 2.13, we show the maximum overhead represented by com-

munication across different merging and granularity configurations in such a high-

latency scenario (500 cycles).

### 2.7 Discussion

Early-stage accelerator design through function merging, based on the optimized se-

lection of merged and non-merged, hardware-mapped functions and loops, opens an

exciting research space that promises to benefit performance and area/latency trade-

offs. AccelMerger can enable lower, system-level data communication, with a focus on

interconnect latency. It allows designers to explore accelerators of varying granulari-

ties without deep application knowledge, as the choice of accelerators is not fixed by

the structure of an application’s source code. Experimental results show up to 16.7×

performance improvement over software-only implementations, and 1.91× on average

over state-of-the-art HW/SW partitioning tools. In future work, we plan to extend

AccelMerger’s SoC-level communication analysis, apply it for cross-application merges

and add power models to its repertoire.

In the next chapter, we will explore the potential of function merging to improve

energy savings. We will also study the impact of different function merging design

choices, such as the IR representation (SSA or not), local vs. global merging tradeoffs,

alignment, and post-code-generation models.

## 3

## Guac: Energy-Aware Coarse-Grained

## Merged Accelerators from LLVM-IR

Designing accelerators for resource- and power-constrained applications is a daunting

task. High-level Synthesis (HLS) addresses these constraints through resource sharing,

an optimization at the HLS binding stage that maps multiple operations to the same

functional unit.

60


<!-- Page 76 -->


However, resource sharing is often limited to reusing instructions within a basic

block. Instead of searching globally for the best control and dataflow graphs (CDFGs)

to combine, it is constrained by existing instruction mappings and schedules.

Coarse-grained function merging (CGFM) at the intermediate representation (IR)

level can reuse control and dataflow patterns without dealing with the post-scheduling

complexity of mapping operations onto functional units, wires, and registers. The

merged functions produced by CGFM can be translated to RTL by HLS, yielding

Coarse Grained Merged Accelerators (CGMAs). CGMAs are especially profitable

across applications with similar data- and control-flow patterns. Prior work has used

CGFM to generate CGMAs without regard for which CGFM algorithms best opti-

mize area, power, and energy costs.

We propose , an energy-aware and SSA-based (static single assignment) CGMA

generation methodology. implements a novel ensemble of cost models for eﬀicient

CGMA generation. We also show that CGFM algorithms using SSA form to merge

control- and dataflow graphs outperform prior non-SSA CGFM designs. We demon-

strate significant area, power, and energy savings with respect to the state of the art.

In particular, more than doubles energy savings with respect to the closest related

work while using a strong resource-sharing baseline.

3.1 Motivation

Manual accelerator designs attempt to reuse fine-grained control and dataflow ap-

plication patterns through the design of processing elements (PEs). Such manual

implementations can be found in cutting-edge domains such as deep learning and

robotics30,63,60. These multi-purpose accelerators greatly benefit from area and power

61


<!-- Page 77 -->


optimizations due to the large number of impacted applications. On the other hand,

automated HLS-level resource sharing28,4 uses analytical models that assume a spe-

cific cost per operation. These works do not study the models’ impact on the acceler-

ator design’s quality. The lack of model studies is due to the multi-layered nature of

the HLS stages, including allocation, scheduling, and binding. Instruction cost mod-

els, when trained statistically, cannot minimize an objective function representing

HLS allocation, scheduling, and binding to understand functional unit reuse prof-

itability. Instead, a cost model mapping IR-level instruction characteristics to accel-

erator characteristics, e.g., power, performance, and area, is built and used as part of

the HLS process when deciding which functional units to reuse. In the related work,

not much attention has been paid to the mismatch between modeling instructions and

modeling functional units. Models are rarely discussed at all in the context of eﬀicient

HLS resource sharing.

Resource sharing works at fine granularity, finding functional units without struc-

tural conflicts that inhibit reuse. Conflict-free reused chains of functional units accel-

erate small, semantically equivalent dataflow graphs scheduled for different cycles. In

our experiments with state-of-the-art HLS and physical design tools, we find that this

kind of resource sharing reduces energy consumption by 45.79% with respect to accel-

erators not benefiting from resource sharing. (See Section 3.3.2 and Section 3.6.2)

Resource sharing, however, has a myopic view of what needs to be reused post-

scheduling. It looks at accelerator reuse not from the perspective of dataflow, control

flow, or input/output reuse but from a functional unit and structural conflict per-

spective. Some accelerator merging tools have sought to address this problem. Re-

confAST37 produces merged accelerators at the loop level in a front-end compiler

(clang), but at such a high level, optimization support is limited. AccelMerger5 lever-

62


<!-- Page 78 -->


ages the function merging by sequence alignment (FMSA) algorithm developed in

the related work52. AccelMerger works at LLVM’s intermediate representation (IR)

level to provide coarse-grained function merging (CGFM), which merges functions

and their call graphs. AccelMerger takes advantage of LLVM’s rich framework for

target-independent interprocedural optimization rather than working on the abstract

syntax tree.

These accelerator merging tools introduce a new way of designing accelerators that

are more programmable than monolithic accelerators in that they can accelerate more

than one top-level function or application. We call them CGMA, standing for coarse-

grained merged accelerators. They are less programmable than finer-grained recon-

figurable architectures, which spend significant area for functional unit (FU) and in-

terconnect programmability. Finer-grained reconfigurable architectures suffer from

significant communication overheads since they accelerate small control and dataflow

patterns. A CGMA can approach the performance of the original monolithic acceler-

ators from which it derives while consuming only a fraction of their total energy and

area. CGFM can produce energy and area savings only for accelerators representing

similar CDFGs. This similarity requirement puts pressure on the CGFM technique to

better understand the impact of local merging decisions on end-to-end energy savings.

In this work, we develop CGFM models aimed at eﬀicient CGMA design, and we

identify the best CGFM algorithms for high CGMA energy savings. We choose en-

ergy savings as a proxy for co-optimizing power, performance, and area. An HLS tool

can produce a monolithic accelerator starting from a function’s high-level or IR-level

representation. After selecting and merging a pair of related functions, we use HLS to

produce a merged accelerator for the pair.

Few prior works can merge at such coarse granularities. To the best of our knowl-

63


<!-- Page 79 -->


edge, the closest is AccelMerger5, which relies on the FMSA IR algorithm for merg-

ing. That approach is limited in three key regards: 1) AccelMerger does not weight

the instructions to be prioritized for merging in terms of their impact for area or en-

ergy savings, but instead applies a uniform weighting on the instruction types to be

merged; 2) AccelMerger uses only one weighting of instructions per merge, which

significantly limits profitability, since different linear models are more effective for

different accelerator characteristics; 3) AccelMerger’s non-SSA code representation

sometimes leads to prohibitive overheads. Instead of SSA’s phi instructions (mapped

to multiplexers by HLS), it generates extra memory instructions, from which HLS

produces expensive accelerator scratchpad accesses.

Prior work on CGMA does not analyze the potential of merging models to generate

more area-eﬀicient accelerator designs5,37. Furthermore, optimization for energy eﬀi-

ciency has been outside the scope of prior CGMA research because of the long latency

of HLS and physical design flows.

In this work, we propose , a novel compiler-based approach for merging accelerators

using multiple non-uniform merging models. We integrate SalSSA50, a state-of-the-art

CGFM approach, with our statistical cost model for energy usage. Our energy model

is trained on post-physical-design estimates, improving its decision-making capabil-

ities during the merge operation to achieve better energy savings. In this study, we

provide inter- and intra-application accelerator merges for a mix of 16 synthesizable

applications from various domains, such as linear algebra, machine learning, and sig-

nal processing. We also provide deeper post-physical-design analysis for power and

device resource consumption, comparing the related work5 with our novel solution.

Overview of results that motivate the solution. When applied to an FPGA tar-

get using a strong resource sharing baseline, reduces LUTs by 7.04%, Flip-Flops (FF)

by 11.17%, and energy consumption by 17.08% on average. By contrast, the closest

related work only improves energy savings by 7.38%, LUTs by 1.06%, and FFs by

2.01%. We demonstrate these results with high accuracy over 16 applications in an

LLVM-to-bitstream setup using a dataset of 10986 merged accelerators.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• Energy-Aware CGFM for CGMAs. We implement a two-step energy-saving

strategy. First, we use arithmetic-, control- and memory-centric CGFM models

to address different bottlenecks in the merged function IR. Second, we select

the final merged function version through an ensemble model that chooses the

most profitable function for acceleration based on LLVM instruction savings.

Related works on coarse-grained and fine-grained accelerator merging abstract

away later synthesis stages, such as physical design, and rely on HLS-level qual-

ity of result estimates. As highlighted in13, HLS-level estimates can be highly

unreliable even for area, with 125% LUT and 98% Flip-Flop mean relative error

(MRE). To create energy-eﬀicient merged accelerators with high confidence in

the quality of results, provides an automated tool flow from high-level C/C++

### 3.3 Background

3.3.1 High Level Synthesis

High Level Synthesis translates high-level code like C/C++ to Verilog or VHDL. Its

stages typically include Allocation, Scheduling, Binding and RTL generation18,36,22.

We focus on the first three of these since the last stage just translates from the HLS

internal representation of functional units and registers to RTL.

Allocation uses device operation modeling to produce an initial estimate of the area

required by an accelerator, especially in terms of functional units.

Scheduling is the phase in which the HLS tool distributes operations across cycles,

taking into account their dependencies. Dependent instructions are chained together

within the same cycle if they do not violate a target cycle time. In this step the Con-

trol Logic of the accelerator is generated, typically as a finite state machine. Neither

allocation nor scheduling has a concept of functional units on which operations will be

scheduled.

Binding constitutes the mapping of operations onto functional units. In this step,

HLS executes the resource sharing optimization by mapping multiple operations onto

the same functional unit if they are not executed in the same cycle. If the dataflow

style of the reused functional unit chain is identical to a previously bound operation

chain, no multiplexing is needed. However, input and output operands usually need

to be routed differently, and expensive multiplexers need to be used. For this reason,

only long latency instructions or chains thereof are reused.

3.3.4 Function Merging by Sequence Alignment

FMSA overview. FMSA52 was the first CGFM algorithm able to merge arbitrary

non-identical pairs of functions introduced with the goal of reducing code size. It was

later used in the context of high level synthesis5 for area reduction (AccelMerger).

We now focus on the FMSA flow at the LLVM IR level. The algorithm consists of

three major stages: choosing which functions to merge, producing the merged func-

tion, and estimating the merging profitability.

Function Pairing. In this chapter, we perform merging across multiple applica-

tions and we merge all pairs of functions in the input applications since some pairings

might be profitable only for some techniques and not for others. This pairing is differ-

ent than in the previous chapter since the goal is to strictly evaluate the improvement

in the merging techniques, both for accelerators that were already profitable as well as

those that were not (and will potentially become profitable).

Function Linearization. For a given pair of functions, merging them requires iden-

73


<!-- Page 89 -->


tifying similar code segments in the two functions that can profitably be merged. To

this end, FMSA52 first linearizes the input functions, representing the CFG as a se-

quence of instructions.

Alignment. Then the Needleman-Wunsch (NW) sequence alignment algorithm

identifies regions of similarity between the two functions. The alignment algorithm

is applied to the linearized sequences of the whole input functions. The NW algo-

rithm allows weighting each operation. In this work, our alignment models provide

the NW weighting of instructions. Finally, the resulting alignment is used to generate

the merged function.

Code Generation. During code generation, the list of parameters from both func-

tions is also merged using a greedy algorithm that tries to merge as many parameters

as possible. Parameters of the same type are shared between the functions, without

necessarily keeping their original order. The merged list of parameters also includes

an extra function identifier. All the calling sites for the input functions are also mod-

ified to point to the newly merged functions with the right parameter order and origi-

nal function identifier.

New Basic Blocks for Contiguous Aligned and Unaligned Instructions. Once the

function definition has been created, the control-flow graph of the merged function

is produced by traversing both the input functions and the aligned sequence. The

merged control-flow graph uses the function identifier for control flow divergence

where the two functions differ, but converges to the same basic block where they

are similar. Operand selection is also introduced where two merged instructions have

different operands. Finally, FMSA applies an SSA reconstruction algorithm on the

merged function.

We believe CGFM-based CGMA generation tools should leverage the flow from

74


<!-- Page 90 -->


alignment through code generation to apply different alignment models, producing

different versions of the merged function. Owing to the nature of sequence alignment

algorithms such as NW, these alignment models are linear. However, after code gener-

ation we have the freedom to evaluate the quality of the IR with more sophisticated,

non-linear models, able to extract more information about accelerator power and area

characteristics by analyzing function-level characteristics such as number of instruc-

tion counts for each instruction type. The potential for such alignment and code gen-

eration models is explored for the first time in Guac.

SSA-Level Limitations. A major limitation in FMSA is its inability to handle phi

nodes, a core feature of the SSA form. In order to work around this limitation, FMSA

performs register demotion (register-to-memory) in all functions prior to linearization,

replacing all phi nodes with a stack-based store-load mechanism. This process tends

to create larger functions, however, lowering the quality of the function merging optimization,

as stores and loads corresponding to phi instructions can be merged against non-phi-related

loads and stores. Extra unaligned loads and stores consequently add a significant

overhead when mapping those instructions to functional units at the allocation step

of HLS. We discuss in Section 3.3.5 how to address this limitation, and we show in

Section 3.4.1 why merging phi nodes and control-flow-related instructions is relevant

for accelerator merging.

CGFM for CGMAs. AccelMerger5 uses FMSA as part of infrastructures for merged

accelerator design based on abstract, post HLS LUT estimates, without considering

FMSA’s potential for power reduction, nor breaking down the benefits of FMSA when

applying it to reduce different resource types or power consumption. As indicated

in Figure 3.2B, with AccelMerger, full data and control paths can be reused, including

registers and functional units. This reuse across the CDFG allows reducing the number

75


<!-- Page 91 -->


of multiplexers when there is a match in the control flow. Some of the savings in

CDFG reuse, however, are hindered due to overhead memory operations that FMSA

cannot transform back into phi instructions, since it performs merging in the non-SSA

format, and when functions are aligned, the components of phi instructions get aligned

with other instructions. We highlight this issue in Figure 3.2B with the red (aligned

but not profitable in this case) load (L) unit. Even though this is the result of aligning

the load instruction against the phi instruction, it results in extra store functional

units later in the design of the top function.

3.3.5 SalSSA and HyFM

SalSSA50 is a CGFM algorithm focused on improving FMSA code generation by

supporting the SSA representation. It avoids the code bloating problem introduced by

register demotion and increases the chances of generating profitable merged functions.

SalSSA’s code generator achieves this by treating phi nodes as special instructions,

excluding them from function alignment since in most cases FMSA would miss-align

the equivalent alloca, store, and load operations. This leads in practice to more saved

instructions. Theoretically, there are cases when FMSA will merge the alloca, load

and store instructions corresponding to the phi instructions correctly against other

phi-related alloca, loads and stores. SalSSA tends to save more because such perfect

phi matches in non-SSA format are unlikely, and even not merging phi instructions at

all is more easily mapped onto multiplexers at synthesis time.

While SalSSA, like FMSA, tries to find an optimal alignment globally across all the

instructions of the merged functions, HyFM51 emphasizes local basic block merges.

HyFM first tries to find the best match of basic blocks according to static instruction

count similarity (fingerprint comparison) and then merges instructions within basic

76


<!-- Page 92 -->


blocks. The advantage of this technique is not only that it reduces sequence alignment

execution time, but also that it is guaranteed to reduce the number of branches in

the function’s control flow, since every basic block ends with a branch. This reduces

the number of predicated instruction executions in the equivalent accelerators and

control-related logic. The disadvantage of this approach is that merges are not global

across all basic blocks, so an opportunity is missed to maximize function-wide area or

power savings.

3.4 Guac

3.4.1 CGFM for accelerator energy eﬀiciency

Alignment and post-code-generation energy model. The main shortcoming in the

related work is that CGFM techniques do not merge for energy savings. There are

two possible approaches to making CGFM energy-savings-aware. One way is by using

alignment models. Algorithms like Needleman-Wunsch (NW) can align sequences

with a linear model, attributing a cost to each instruction type. The result is that

NW finds the alignment with the lowest cost due to the algorithm’s optimality guarantees.

The second possible energy model considered in this chapter is post-code-generation.

It is applied on the resulting CDFG after aligning two functions. Post-code-generation

models evaluate the potential energy savings directly using the features of the merged

function instead of some abstract representation of the function (e.g., the sequences

used in the sequence alignment algorithm).

We use alignment-time merging to create multiple versions of a merged function,

while taking account of the accelerator back end. Then we apply a code-generation-time

statistical model based on random forests to select the accelerator version most likely

77


<!-- Page 93 -->


to generate energy savings.

Control, memory, and arithmetic alignment models. Alignment models are analytical,

and we use them to emphasize saving either control, memory, or arithmetic instructions.

The intuition for this type of model is that array-style architectures, including FPGAs,

have limited resources per slice (e.g., multiplexers, flip-flops, lookup tables, or DSPs).

The per-slice logic is under-utilized when an application is memory-, compute- or

control-intense. Still, a good balance of resource usage allows HLS to map more operations

per slice, reducing routing and multiplexing costs. In the three alignment-time models,

we put a higher weight (twice that on the other instructions) on either of these instruction

types.

These savings are represented in Figure 3.2C in the proper merging prioritization

of the high-cost division, multiplication, and memory instructions. The diﬀiculty here

is that modeling needs to operate from a higher level of abstraction than resource

sharing from the IR level. Resource sharing benefits from accurate knowledge about

the mappings between operations and functional units, whereas at the IR level, we

need to use both per-operation models to guide the merging process, as well as overall

evaluations of the generated CDFG in the IR (post-code-generation models).

For the control models, we prioritize the merging of all the LLVM branch instructions

(conditional, unconditional, direct, and indirect), phi instructions, compare instructions

(cmp and fcmp), and the switch statement. For the memory model we include load,

store, alloca, fence, extractelement, extractvalue, getelemptr, insertvalue, insertelement,

and shufflevector. For the arithmetic model, we include all floating point, integer,

boolean, bitwise and casting operations. The reason for using these specific models is

the pressure each type of instruction puts on the FPGA slices. Implementing CGMAs

for a target other than FPGA, such as ASIC, will benefit from further fine-tuning of

The need for post-code-generation models. In our experiments and in related work

on guiding IR-time optimizations for accelerator back ends19,22, we find that no single

alignment model can improve merges across applications. There are three reasons why

this is so. First, different application mixtures create different bottlenecks. Second,

alignment algorithms rely on linear models to determine the weight of an operation

whereas the process of mapping instructions to hardware is highly non-linear. Third,

many overhead instructions, such as extra selects for the operands of merged instructions,

are not known at alignment time, but are available after code generation.

Guac’s post-code-generation random forest uses the number of saved instructions of

each instruction type, compared to the original functions, to predict energy savings.

This prediction is performed on the three versions of the merged function with either

control, memory, or arithmetic focus. We collect a dataset of true energy savings

(target variable) on a thousand post-place-and-route merged accelerators and their

operation-level savings (features) to train the random forest model.

instructions against other phi-related instructions. An FMSA-based phi misalignment,

therefore, has an overhead of at least the 120 LUTs corresponding to an alloca, 37 ×

Whenever any of the phi-related instructions are merged against non-phi-related

In this chapter, we analyze SSA-based CGFM techniques that avoid high area and

energy penalties. Based on this analysis, as well as our experimental results, we show

is reflected in Figure 3.2C since the phi instruction is left intact, enabling the reuse of

Global, SSA-based merging feasibility. The first novel CGFM technique we evaluate

for this chapter is SalSSA, which performs global merging like FMSA, but operates

directly on the SSA representation of the code. Compared with FMSA, SalSSA reduces

by19.55%. This results in less circuitry related to memory operations as well as reductions

3.5 Implementation

In this section, we describe our end-to-end solution. Figure 3.5 shows the process by

which we extract merged accelerators from the high-level source code, how merged

functions are being produced and how we map both merged and non-merged functions

to accelerators.

The flow for merging consists of a front end that collects important information

about the application, including generating the testbench for the cosimulated functions.

Then the middle end step merges functions with the goal of achieving large area

savings while trading off the minimum amount of performance. The back end converts

84


<!-- Page 100 -->


both merged and non-merged functions to RTL via HLS. Then it performs technology

mapping and place-and-route for accurate FPGA area and power data collection.

Our experiments measure area savings, latency overhead, and energy savings with

respect to fine-grained HLS resource sharing. Specifically we measure CGMA improvement

for two functions f1 and f2 on resource Y using the formula ICGMA,Y = Cconcat,Y(f1,f2) CCGMA,Y(f1,f2).

Since we are directly comparing the merged accelerators, we measure latency improvement

instead of overhead since the HLS layer sometimes trades area savings for latency and

power improvements.

The main focus in this chapter is on improving CGMA energy eﬀiciency. We focus

on the energy component of the used resources. The selection of a device that is a

good match for a given application, so that the dynamic component of energy dominates

the design, is outside the scope of this work.

3.5.1 Standard Optimizations and Co-simulation

The source code is compiled down to LLVM IR. Standard optimizations among -O1,-O2

and -O3 are applied on the compiled IR. In our experiments, we find that -O1 creates

an IR that produces the lowest area and power consumption across the -Ox configurations,

allowing the HLS tools to fine-tune code for FPGA targets. All the reported merged

accelerators, including baseline concatenation-based accelerators, are produced with

-O1 on the result of the merged function as well as on the input functions.

Our HLS tool requires a .xml file to specify the input values to use for the co-simulated

functions. Given the large number of merged functions to evaluate, we automate the

generation of this .xml file by creating an LLVM instrumentation pass and a run-time

library.

### 3.7 Related Work

Most coarse grained merging for accelerator design is occurring in the context of

manual code analysis and acceleration60,9,30,63. In this work, we improve automated

96


<!-- Page 112 -->


coarse-grained merging to further motivate the use of coarse-grained accelerator merging.

The main related works in coarse-grained accelerator merging are AccelMerger5

and ReconfAST37. They rely on analytical models to provide merging information

early in accelerator design, while in this chapter we focus on a highly accurate C/LLVM-to-bitstream

approach. ReconfAST implements the merging optimization in the C-front-end layer

of clang (pre-LLVM), which makes it specific to a single high-level language, and

less likely to benefit from mainstream compiler optimization research. Also, IRs are

simpler and more amenable to optimizations like CGFM than high-level languages.

For example, control flow in the IR is handled with branch and phi instructions,

whereas at a high-level there are many control-related constructs, such as while, for,

do while, if and switch statements.

There is a large body of work on resource sharing that have shaped the area and

power optimizations implemented in HLS and physical design tools4,68,64,67,28,39,10.

Even though some related works discuss PPA estimation14,13,81,5,76,23 these models

are rarely used for compiler optimization and not with the goal of interprocedural

optimization aimed at CGMA generation. Cycle-accurate accelerator simulation literature

has used linear operation-level optimizations but coarse grained accelerator merging

is out of the scope of these works53,54. CGFM-based CGMA accelerator works37,5 by

contrast contain no contributions on models either at alignment time nor at post-code-generation

time.

FMSA, HyFM and SalSSA52,51,50 are LLVM compilation transformations aimed

code reduction. These techniques use the CPU ISA (linear) model for code size out of

the box to guide the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm in finding an optimal alignment.

Since LLVM lacks FPGA cost models, we implement our own cost models and replace

candidate selection. Since HLS stages are much more complicated than mapping IR

97


<!-- Page 113 -->


to some back-end CPU ISA, we use an ensemble of models emphasizing either control,

data or memory instructions for merging.

### 3.8 Discussion

This chapter focuses on optimizing accelerator merging techniques and models for

higher area and energy savings. Our evaluation indicates average improvements in

LUTs of 7.04%, 11.17% in FFs, with a penalty of 0.07% in DSPs and energy savings

of 17.08%, respectively, with respect to a strong resource-sharing baseline. This represents

a significant improvement with respect to state-of-the-art CGFM-based CGMA generation,

which improves energy savings by only 7.38%, LUTs by 1.06%, and FFs by 2.01%.

Finally, our post-code-generation and alignment models bring our solution EnsembleGuac

close to an exhaustive configuration ExhaustGuac, which achieves 18.4% energy savings

and similar area improvements. These results motivate future work on enabling more

transition of compiler techniques to the research field of HLS and work on enabling

function level instead of operation level models in the alignment algorithms.

Thanks to EnsembleGuac, we can design EDSE tools that generate eﬀicient merged

accelerators from the IR. We saw that statistical models can help in designing high-quality

merged accelerators. Next, we explore the relationship between IR cost models for

hardware accelerators and overall system-on-chip EDSE.

## 4

## Towards Highly-Accurate Early-Stage

## Hardware-Software Partitioning

Early-Stage Design Space Exploration (EDSE) is emerging as a new design automation

branch to cope with the increasing complexity of software-hardware co-design. EDSE

allows the discovery of functions worth accelerating in the source code of an application.

As a result, the hardware designer can commit to a hardware-software partitioning of

99


<!-- Page 115 -->


an application. It is not the role of EDSE to perform detailed accelerator, CPU, or

interconnect design but to guide the hardware designer toward the most important

functions with tools better than standard software profiling methods (e.g., gprof).

We analyze the sources of inaccuracy in existing EDSE tools. They lack precision

because of a focus on analytical models built by experts via trial and error. Their

ability to extrapolate to new applications is limited because they fail to separate

training from inference. We also analyze the end-to-end impact of choosing different

models in an EDSE solution. We find that non-linear models are important in increasing

accuracy and approaching optimal accelerator selection. By simplifying typical EDSE

flows, we demonstrate a highly accurate prediction method for latency (2.62% error)

and area (6.63% error) compared to related work (4% and 45.5% error for latency and

area). We reduce the distance to optimum to 6.04% and 18.79% area and latency-wise

respectively from 38.1% and 93.6%. We demonstrate our results training on the 19

MachSuite applications and kernels and testing on a complex application, the H.264

decoder. Finally, we demonstrate that our solution can solve EDSE problems 50×

larger than related EDSE tools.

4.1 Motivation

Late DSE is a consolidated field in design automation with tools like gem5-Aladdin55

and gem5-SALAM53 used to simulate SoCs with CPUs and accelerators. These tools

rely on a tedious and error-prone process to partition the application for CPU and

accelerator execution. They also rely on the hardware designer to convert code to

a format with simple data structures such as arrays and no hardware side effects.

Late-DSE requires many iterations implementing data communication between the

100


<!-- Page 116 -->


CPU and accelerator as well as optimizing the hardware-related code, all in a post-partitioning

stage of SoC design.

Deciding how to partition code, however, especially in the case of complex applications,

is still an open problem. Tools like RegionSeeker80, Trireme78, and AccelSeeker79

have pioneered an approach to the application partitioning problem under the name

of Early-Stage Design Space Exploration (EDSE). EDSE promises to provide hardware-software

partitioning feedback starting from source code and high-level architectural constraints.

One major flaw inherited by EDSE from Late-DSE is a reliance on expert analytical

models to produce early-stage estimates for hardware latency and area. These expert

models estimate the costs of instructions and are the basis for making coarser granularity

estimates for basic blocks, regions, functions, and function hierarchies. Those estimated

costs are hardcoded in the source code of the EDSE and Late-DSE tools. In the case

of Late-DSE, since simulation tools emulate many of the stages of High-Level-Synthesis

(HLS) flows, they manage to achieve remarkable accuracy on both latency and area.

These stages include loop pipelining, phi-node and memory instruction removal, buffering,

and fusion. These Late-DSE steps are possible when the source code is synthesizable

and its hardware and software partitions have been chosen. EDSE, however, must

achieve reasonable accuracy without being able to reproduce in great detail the HLS

steps. It is not clear from the related work whether building an EDSE that extrapolates

to new applications is possible, with what accuracy, and what are the optimality

limitations of the EDSE solutions.

This chapter studies the impact of these inaccuracies on selecting accelerator candidates.

The chapter’s contributions are as follows:

• Sensitivity analysis. Section 4.2 highlights the following three key sources of

inaccuracy for selection-based EDSE. 1) We show that traditionally used linear

evaluated in Section 4.5.2. 3) We mitigate the suboptimal effects of expert

### 4.2 Background

A typical EDSE flow79,80,78,5,26,81 is represented in Figure 4.1. The EDSE problem

is: How can we provide useful hardware/software partitioning information to the

designer, using the application source code, standard dynamic profiling information,

and a resource budget, without using HLS or Late-DSE tools? EDSE tools apply

expert linear latency and area models to dynamic and static instruction counts to

102


<!-- Page 118 -->


*Figure 4.1: Common EDSE framework in the related work.*

come up with predictions of required accelerator area and latency at larger granularities,

i.e., functions79,5 and loops26,81.

This requires compiler-based analysis, as highlighted in Figure 4.1 part B 79,26,81,

to extract dynamic and static counts per instruction type. To build those coarser

granularity estimates, EDSE partially emulates HLS-related stages such as allocation,

scheduling, and binding programmatically. EDSE also includes models for how data

gets transferred between the CPU and accelerator components of the system to filter

high-overhead fine-granularity accelerators or accelerators with high data-transfer-to-computation

ratio79. An example interconnect model is for the AXI-bus with its bandwidth and

latency.

Then, design-space-exploration-related code (Figure 4.1 part C) finds the mixture

of functions that yields the most benefit, given an area budget. Related work is either

focused on the DSE component with little consideration for model impact in EDSE

accuracy79,78,80,81,5,26, or it is focused on the models with little or no consideration for

EDSE58,16,62,70,34.

103


<!-- Page 119 -->


The output of a typical EDSE tool is a selection of functions to be accelerated

by the designer (with the remainder of the functions to be run on a CPU) and an

estimate of the required resources and overall latency of the proposed partitioning. To

produce this estimate, EDSE tools also resort to the same area and latency models to

estimate the final execution time of the application when running it on an accelerator+CPU

hybrid, especially if the application is in very early stages and in non-synthesizable

format.

Expert models used in EDSE tools (and also in Late-DSE tools) tend to have these

issues:

Underfitting

Expert models are not achieved by statistical fitting a representative set of points, but

by manually modifying model weights to fit the data. That leads to both less-than-ideal

expected speedup benefits for the acceleration of the selected functions and EDSE

suboptimality with respect to optimal accelerated points that would otherwise be

found with accurate hardware knowledge about the functions. An example would be

the hard-coded cost of each instruction type in AccelSeeker’s open source repository

both area as well as latency-wise.∗

Overfitting

Since there is no discussion of training and testing in the EDSE related works (and

also in many Late-DSE works), expert/trial-and-error models may well be developed

on the same applications as those on which they are tested. This leads to the false

∗In function getDelayEstim in ﬁle AccelSeeker/AccelSeeker.h in AccelSeeker’s GitHub repository GiorgioZacharo/AccelSeeker.

104


<!-- Page 120 -->


expectation that these tools extrapolate well to new applications. We evaluate this

limitation in Section 4.5.2.

Linearity

EDSE tools typically rely on linear models, assigning one weight per instruction.

However, the many complex layers of HLS transformations are highly non-linear (for

example, redundancy elimination techniques and data-flow optimizations applied to

code by HLS).

Related work shows that linear models do not perform well even in post-HLS,

pre-place-and-route stages70,16,58 on problems aimed at fine tuning HLS pragmas

rather than the earlier-stage goal of identifying functions for acceleration. This limitation

was also studied for accelerator latency modeling62 with pre-HLS total dynamic instruction

counts insuﬀicient for high accuracy. Our experience with EDSE tools relying on

linear models (Sections 4.5.1 and 4.5.3) is also that they tend not to perform very well

on early-stage information, especially pre-HLS information, such as the application

source code and profiling information.

The related work that best captures the goals of the EDSE problem is AccelSeeker79.

AccelSeeker does not require annotations on the code unlike derivative tools such as

Trireme78 which requires region input and output annotations, or Hypermapper41

which requires a total refactoring of the application into a domain specific language.

AccelSeeker also has a flexible concept of granularity being able to select for acceleration

functions and hierarchies of functions. Other related works81,26,80 are constrained

at the loop or region level and overlook important fine-granularity issues such as

CPU-accelerator data-transfer and invocation overheads. We include AccelSeeker in

our analysis in addition to a hardware-accurate configuration as described in Section 4.4.

4.3 Accura-EDSE, our proposed EDSE design

In our approach termed Accura-EDSE, we address the interaction between optimization

(MILP-based) and inaccuracies inherent to the inputs of the EDSE problem.

*Figure 4.2 shows how Accura-EDSE updates the flow of Figure 4.1. A statistical*

model replaces Part A. Part B eliminates code transformations and critical path

analysis that are specific to the brand and version of the HLS tool being modeled.

Instead, Accura-EDSE applies statistical models to static and dynamic instruction

counts, producing area and latency estimates at the function level. This simplification

means that a new type of accelerator or technology node can be adopted just by

retraining the model instead of having to reverse engineer the accelerator synthesis

106


<!-- Page 122 -->


flow and emulate programatically those steps in the EDSE tool. Finally, Figure 4.2

Parts C and D show that instead of adhering to ad-hoc EDSE implementations, we

propose a novel MILP-based solution.

4.3.1 Addressing underfitting, overfitting and linearity problems in expert mod-

els

Accelerator latency. To avoid underfitting, we predict the hardware latency HW(f) =

CALLS(f) ∗HWone_call(f) of each function f. We use dynamic instruction counts for one

call of f to build a model for HWone_call(f). CALLS(f) is available in the application

dynamic instrumentation during the early stages of design. In our experiments, just

predicting HWone_call(f), while using the true value of CALLS(f), dramatically increases

the accuracy of HW(f) estimates. In fact, we observe that even linear latency models

deliver close to 97.3% accuracy for HW(f) when we focus on predicting HWone_call(f)

and leverage the true CALLS(f) information. The most sophisticated models that

try to predict HW(f) struggle to achieve high accuracy, even for CPU latency34, but

especially for accelerator latency71,70,58,16.

Area Estimates. For predicting AREA(f), we noticed that the linearity problem is

important and that linear models such as linear regression and Lasso tend to lead to

EDSE inaccuracy. To address these problems, we use a model that is able to exploit

non-linearities in area prediction, namely random forests. In Section 4.5.3, we show a

marked increase in solution optimality (area and latency improvements due to optimal

selection) as well as highly accurate reports to the EDSE tool user. As discussed in

Section 4.5.1, non-linear models also mitigate area budget violations that occur in

tools that rely on linear models. Experiments with other non-linear models, such

as the Multilayer-Perceptron (MLP), did not yield increased accuracy on this data.

107


<!-- Page 123 -->


Random forests are more interpretable and can be more quickly trained than MLP.

Static and Dynamic Features. For predictions of both HWone_call(f) and AREA(f),

we use a dataframe with 64 features, corresponding to the 64 LLVM instruction types.

For HWone_call(f), we use hierarchical dynamic instruction counts for one call of f

(including direct and indirect callees). For AREA(f), we use the hierarchical static

instruction count corresponding to f.

Overfitting and Underfitting. To avoid overfitting both for AREA(f) and HW(f)

on a set of applications, we train our models on the MachSuite47 benchmarks and

perform testing on a well known application, the H.264 decoder32 proposed in the

related work to further research in design automation problems such as EDSE. We

have measured the misleading effect of overfitting in related work when a training and

testing methodology is not used and we present the results in Section 4.5.2. We avoid

underfitting by using statistical learning at the function level, rather than adjusting

per-instruction weights via trial-and-error or expert methodology.

CPU latency. CPU latency SW(f) for each f is easily obtained in early design stages

by running the application on a CPU with a standard profiler. In Accura-EDSE, we

collect SW(f) using standardized LLVM-based profiling, attached to the source code

via metadata. This gives the true SW(f) for each function.

accounts for the penalties of invoking the accelerator multiple times (latency) and the

Objective function description

The first term of the objective function (hwvi · hwi + swvi · swi) in Equation 4.1 expresses

application execution time, given a mapping of functions, either to the CPU or to

accelerators. The second term accounts for data transfers to, and invocations of,

accelerators.

The MILP solver will try to set as many of the variables hwvi, swvi and frontierij

as it can to 0, since each is associated with a cost. The constraints prevent it from

setting all variables to 0. This formulation effectively handles the call graph and

hierarchical hardware synthesis. We next describe how the combination of Equations 4.2

and 4.3 achieves this effect.

Constraints description

Equation 4.2 enforces a software or hardware realization of the top function. This

constraint combines well with the hierarchical realization of the hardware constraint

in Equation 4.3.

Equation 4.3 requires that if function i is realized in software, each of its callees j

is also realized, either in software or hardware. If a function is realized in hardware,

this constraint doesn’t affect it, which is the desired modelling since the hwi and areai

constants are hierarchical. Equation 4.4 causes the expected behavior for the frontierij

variable, i.e., if caller i is realized in hardware, callee j is realized in hardware too.

Finally, Equation 4.3.2 sets the accelerator area budget.

### 4.6 Related Work

A goal of EDSE tools is to select the most feasible functions for acceleration to maximize

performance subject to resource constraints such as area and communication constraints.

EDSE selection can be performed using MILP, or other design space exploration

techniques including semi-brute-force algorithms such as independent-set detection79,80

118


<!-- Page 134 -->


or exhaustive design space search81. These EDSE non-MILP79,80 and other MILP-based

related works5,41,81 are focused on software-hardware partitioning, overlooking the

interaction between model accuracy and overall solution optimality and accuracy.

In this work, we compare against79 because of the granularity, system modeling and

degree to which it addresses the EDSE problem (see AccelSeeker discussion in Section 4.2).

By contrast, the focus of late-stage DSE tools55,53 is on detailed point solutions,

which can only be slowly evaluated. Another class of Late-DSE tools is represented

by FARSI3 and Platform Architect61. They are late-stage DSE, even in their agile

execution models, because they rely on existing code partitioning and expert analysis

of each partition to perform system-level DSE. There are tools that trade-off some

EDSE flexibility for closer-to-late-DSE accuracy, behaving more like Late-DSE. Examples

include41 and78, but they require porting the application to a new (often domain

specific) language.

### 4.7 Discussion

In this chapter, we focused on the EDSE accelerator selection problem for systems

with CPU and accelerators. We isolated the effect of expert linear models that train

and test on the same applications, a methodology consistently applied both in the

space of EDSE and Late-DSE. We propose an alternative design with Accura-EDSE,

which has an error as low as 2.6% and 6.6% for latency and area, respectively, while

making EDSE problems up to 83.3× larger than related work feasible in the time

frame of a few minutes.

## 5

## Conclusion

Early-stage non-conventional accelerator discovery through flexible hardware/software

partitioning and merging was mostly believed to be relevant for smaller sub-problems

in early-stage design-space exploration. Some examples are 1) improving the feedback

a designer can get with tools better than those used for software profiling and 2)

the accelerator ranking problem in area-agnostic scenarios. In this thesis, we show

that even the accelerator selection problem can be solved with high accuracy and

120


<!-- Page 136 -->


close-to-optimum solutions. We also show that the EDSE problem can be extended

to search simultaneously for the optimum partitioning at different granularities of

loops, functions, merged loops and functions and merged call graphs. We saw that

acknowledging IR-specific (e.g. the SSA representation) and building powerful models

for the alignment problem can significantly improve the discovery of merged accelerators

at all these granularities.

We believe, that IR research will continue to play a significant role in Early-Stage-DSE

due to the inputs of the problem being high level source code and dynamic profiling.

Novel IRs such as HPVM and MLIR will provide plenty of room at the top to further

detect system-wide opportunities in the early design stages, especially for novel technology

nodes, novel data-types, complex memory hierarchies, pre-existing accelerators and

domain-specific metrics of success in addition to systems with accelerators and CPUs

as seen in this work.

# Improving Scalability of Task-Based Programs

Iulian Brumar, Marc Casas, Miquel Moretó

Barcelona Supercomputing Center ibrumar@bsc.es, marc.casas@bsc.es, miquel.moreto@bsc.es Abstract- In a multi-core era, parallel programming allows further performance improvements, but with an important programmability cost. We envision that the best approach to parallel programming that can exceed the programability, parallelism, power, memory and reliability walls in Computer Architecture is a run-time approach. Many traditional computer architecture concepts can be revisited and applied at the runtime layer [4][5] in a completely transparent way to the programmer. The goal of this work is taking the computer architecture value prediction and dataprefetching concepts inside a runtime environment like OmpSs.

I.INTRODUCTION The main objective of this work is researching if Value Locality exists in state of the art OmpSs programs and if we can use it in order to obtain better execution times.

Value locality is the property of a static instruction to produce the same output given the same input. If, let us say, a hardware sum instruction it is executed twice in a loop, and both times it gets exactly the same inputs, for its second execution we already know that it will generate the same output. However in hardware load instructions, if the input is the same -the addresswe are not sure if it will produce the same result. In this case we can only speculate, but even so it has been shown that in many cases, static loads with same input produce the same output [1].

By using this knowledge, we can build a predictor that will skip those instructions that can be well predicted and feed the depending instructions earlier with the predicted output.

In this work we take this concept to a new level for OmpSs tasks and we can distinguish two sub-objectives:

1) Analyze OmpSs benchmarks predictability. We cannot prove that value locality will lead to performance improvement for all possible programs, but we can at least focus on state of the art applications that have been ported to the OmpSs programming model and see how can the value locality concept be extended to our context.

2) Find the ideal speedup using a value locality predictor. This second objective it is a consequence of the previous one. In the cases where value locality exists, what performance

improvement can be achieved? We will answer this question using simulation tools.

Notice that this is a best case approach in order to discover the limits of the predictability we can have. Also we have to mention that this work was performed with fine grained tasks.

II.RELATED WORK Since the first moments of computer architecture, it has been seen that the dependencies between instructions were a big wall against Instruction Level Parallelism (ILP). A good example of instruction level parallelism is the pipelined processor, which is made of several hardware slots, each one with a specific function. If there are two slots in our processor, namely A and B, an instruction must fulfill both stages in order to complete its execution. We call this an instance of ILP because the processor can have two instructions running at the same time. If we hadn't pipelined the processor every instruction would have executed in time time(A) + time(B) but this technique allows us to execute a instruction in time max(time(A), time(B)).

The problem is that the instruction in the first stage (A) might need the result produced by the oldest instruction in (B). In this case the newest instruction will spend one more cycle in stage A and this is a conflict caused by a Read After Write RAW dependency. Even so, back to the 90's, the architects came with a solution [1]. The idea was to continue the execution of the instructions affected by the conflict speculatively. In our example it means that the instruction in stage A can complete the process in this stage speculating the result of the instruction in stage B, and check if the supposition was correct in the next stage.

Now a very good question would be: How can processors predict well the results of hardware instructions? That issue has been explored in the papers of Lipasti [2] and Sazeides [1] which form the motivational base of this work. In the first one the predictor is implemented in two different processor architectures (the out of order PowerPC and the in order Alpha), while the second article gives a more theoretical approach to the issue explaining computational predictors (explained in more detail in [3]) and context based predictors.
